content.title: Response to Our Reviewers
content.comment:
Dear Reviewers:
      Thanks for your constructive comments in a short reviewing time. The common concern is the definition of our problem.  Here are our explanations: (1) The disjoint regression setting is a particular regression case but it can also be applied to the overlapped problem. In many real-world scenarios,  two overlapped domains usually have the same causal mechanism, their overlapped part does not need generalization. 2) As we claimed in the Introduction, we investigate the typical domain generalization methods and their performance in our disjoint regression setting. To the best of our knowledge,  we are the first to systematically investigate this extreme setting from the perspective of domain generalization. 
       For experiments, we have discussed the SOTA baselines， such as DDG (CVPR 22), and CAD (ICML 22). We will consider adding various datasets in revised version. 
       However, considering the over-low scores, we decide to withdraw our work directly.
       Thanks again for your contribution!

content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think the model setup and problem formulation are not clear. The authors only proposed the objective functions in Section 4 without an explicit explanation of why the domain differs in range. Considering the assumption that the source domains and target domains have a disjoint regression range, what is the factor that caused such a difference? Is it because of the distribution of X or the regression function f? 
Also, for the regression problem, a more general case would be the response range may have some overlap between the source domain and the target domain.  Besides the model setup, the paper is also lack of theoretical analysis. This part can be further strengthened.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the work can be further improved by clarifying the model setup and developing theoretical results regarding how to guarantee the prediction performance for the target domain.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to consider the task of domain generalization in regression, where the range of target variables in the unseen domain are disjoint from those of the seen domains. Then they propose an algorithm to solve this problem.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper has a *lot* of significant weaknesses and I don't think it is ready for publication. I took notes while reading; I will give high-level points but at some point I stopped writing everything down.

First of all, **regression in DG is not new**. Even as far back as Invariant Causal Prediction [1], which was originally intended for causal inference, clearly applies to SEMs with continuous outputs. More recent works such as [2, 3, 4] also consider this problem. The claim of novelty here is simply incorrect.

Generally, the paper tries to give the impression that there is theoretical understanding or justification for many of the explanations or design decisions, when it is clear that none exists. Much of the paper uses pseudo-formal terminology, e.g. "defining" a margin with words and not actually giving a clear definition, using the terms "interpolation" and "extrapolation" as if they have a single definition. The entirety of page 2 is very difficult to understand for this reason.

Along the same lines, there are a *lot* of notational issues that make things difficult to understand or just incorrect. Some of the few I wrote down:

1. First you define $X_1, X_2$, then you use lower case $x_1, x_2$, then you *redefine* $X_1, X_2$

2. The formulation of the objective on page 4 doesn’t make sense, wouldn’t you minimize in expectation? Minimizing over the supremum of individual samples is very clearly not what we would want to do, not that it would even be possible. Also, IPM is an expectation, whereas $x_1, x_2$ are instantiated values.

3. The "sampling bias" definition also does not make sense, and is not a definition.

4. Bottom of page 4, $\widehat {IPM}$ is not the same as IPM. **What are you infimizing over?** 

5. Top of page 5, what does “divergent optimization” mean here? Also, this paragraph makes no sense. Are you assuming that we always receive X values in pairs? What does $f(X_2 | X_1)$ mean? Is this meant to imply that $f$ is a function of $X_1$ and $X_2$? Or that $f(X_1)$ outputs a function which is then applied to $X_2$?

Next, there is no meaningful motivation whatsoever for the objective. It just falls out of nowhere with no real reasoning. Why is the loss defined as the norm, and not the square loss? This is an atypical choice which needs some sort of explanation. Why does the loss get multiplied by the distance? What is this supposed to achieve?

There's also no real justification for the setting considered, where different domains have disjoint target ranges. This is an absurdly strong requirement which needs some sort of explanation. It's not reasonable to just "assume" things out of nowhere and then expect your results to have any real-world applicability.

As an aside, **why are the experiments presented in the main body the test-domain validation set results**? These results are completely meaningless for the task that we care about. Though I appreciate that at least it is clearly indicated in the table, this should appear only in the appendix at best and the actual comparison to other methods should be brought to the main body. But this is relatively minor compared to the over major flaws in this work.

[1] Causal inference using invariant prediction: identification and confidence intervals. Peters et al. 2016

[2] Anchor regression: heterogeneous data meets causality. Rothenhäusler et al. 2018

[3] Domain-Adjusted Regression or: ERM May Already Learn Features Sufficient for Out-of-Distribution Generalization. Rosenfeld et al. 2022

[4] On Invariance Penalties for Risk Minimization. Khezeli et al. 2022

They argue this regression nature renders many, if not all, existing classification based domain generalisation methods, no longer suitable for the domain generalisation regression setting. content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1) a novel setting is introduced;
2) a novel method is proposed for the new setting with improved empirical performance. 

Weakness:
1) the experimental setting is non-ideal. The authors use Cross-Age Celebrity Dataset (CACD) and The Asian Face Age Dataset (AFAD) to estimate the ages. They normalise the labels (ages) to the range of [0,1]. This setting doesn't suit classification methods such as MLDG and many others in the experiment. Even if the classification methods use unnormlised ages as outputs, they may treat ages as categorical, i.e. not utilising the fact that (30-29)<(30-25) that regression method would utilise and be aware.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies domain generalization (DG) problem in regression settings. In particular, different from DG in classification, regression can have disjoint target ranges across domains. The paper proposes a weighted meta-learning strategy for DG in regression, which uses the feature discrepancy in meta-space to calculate the discrepancy between any two domains for weight calculation. The authors perform several regression experiments on standard DG benchmark, demonstrating that the proposed method can improve upon current solutions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength 

+ The setting is interesting and timely. DG is an important problem; yet addressing the regression problem in DG is less explored. The paper did a good job in initiating this interesting setting and providing analysis.

+ The author performed relatively extensive comparisons to current methods spaning different learning categories.

+ The writing and paper structure is good. The paper is easy to follow.

---
# Weaknesses
Unfortunately, there are several major weaknesses that exist in the current paper.

### Setting
The authors described the DGR setting as *"label space of different domains is disjoint in our regression setting"*. However, this does not make sense to me. In DG, there are no limitation to the label distribution between source domain(s) and target domain. They can be matched, mismatched, divergent, or even disjoint (for certain domains). Extending to regression, it should also follow the same setup, rather than limiting the case to only "disjoint". I do not see the reason to have the limitation that  *"label space of different domains"*.  For example, the data collection process can be totally different (e.g., camera setting, lighting condition, etc.) for different age datasets, forming different domains; their label distribution, however, is not required to be exactly disjoint, as the goal is to **generalize** to new domains, rather than **extrapolate** to new target values.

### Experiments

- One obvious drawback is the lack of thorough experiments. The experiments are only done on two (real) age datasets.
1. Regression tasks are very common in real-world and not just exist in vision domain. Current benchmarks should be extended to other domains. For example, NLP (e.g., text similarity), satellite imaging (earth surface temperature), or healthcare (health metrics such as heart rate, blood pressure, etc) domains often involve continuous targets as well as distribution shifts. Even in the vision domain, there are far more tasks that exhibit continuous label space other than just age (e.g., depth, angle, 3D location, etc.). Only evaluating on two age datasets makes the observation not convincing, and one would naturally ask does the method generalize to other domains / tasks.
2. The setting to me is a bit weird -- different domains have completely disjoint age ranges. This is only a special case in DG, as DG has no requirements in label distribution between domains. 

- Even for the task of age estimation, which can be formulated as a regression problem, I believe treating it as a classification task (with a bin size of 1) would also be reasonable. That being said, classification methods in DG can be directly adapted for this task.
1. Although many algorithms are selected, the paper actually failed to compare with *SOTA* DG approaches, including [1, 2] as well as those competitive methods in the DomainBed benchmarks [3], such as CORAL. Some of the algorithms from [3] are selected, yet they have already been proved in [3] that do not deliver better results than ERM. Again, the selected baselines are no longer SOTA, and without comparing to the aforementioned strong baselines, the results are not convincing.
2. In addition to DG approaches, ordinal classification methods would be another natural choice to compare with, especially given this line of works typically consider age estimation as the target task [4-7].

- Moreover, even follow the age estimation tasks, the actual result improvements are rather marginal.
1. Many methods already achieve a VERY low regression errors in the two datasets (e.g., DDG exhibits regression MSE **<0.05** in all tested domains). In terms of age regression, this is already very accurate (average absolute error around 0.3 year). The improvements, however, is pretty marginal.
2. Although Std is provided (this is good), many of the improvements are actaully in the noise range (e.g., std can be as high as 0.01 when the mean MSE is 0.02). This makes the results less interpretable and not meaningful.

- What is the actual computational cost of the proposed method, in terms of both time and memory consumption?

1. I can see that it introduces additional optimization steps during iterations. These can introduce huge computation (both memory and training time) costs, especially when the number of domains and/or number of classes scale up. Can the authors give a complexity analysis of the algorithm?

2. Wall-clock training time comparison as well as memory consumption to other baseline methods would be good.

---
# Reference
[1] Cha et al. SWAD: Domain Generalization by Seeking Flat Minima. 2021.

[2] Arpit et al. Ensemble of averages: Improving model selection and boosting performance in domain generalization. 2021.

[3] Gulrajani et al. In search of lost domain generalization. 2021.

[4] Ordinal regression with multiple output cnn for age estimation. 2016

[5] Deep ordinal regression network for monocular depth estimation. 2018

[6] Rank consistent ordinal regression for neural networks with application to age estimation. 2020

[7] Deep neural networks for rank-consistent ordinal regression based on conditional probabilities. 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity
Good.

Overall the writing is good. The structure is fine. Several typos exist.

## Quality
Fair.

Figures and tables are well presented. Several interesting visualizations.

## Novelty
Fair.

As I mentioned in the weakness part, although the problem itself is interesting and less explore, the setting to me does not make sense and is rather limited. There also exist several major drawbacks in the experiments, making it hard to justify the paper's novelty.

See the above weakness part for details.

## Reproducibility
N/A

Although in the Reproducibility statement, the author claimed that the code is provided (with an anonymous link), there is nothing in the provided link, so I take this as "No code is provided".
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper studied an interesting and under-explored problem - Domain generalization in regression tasks. The topic is interesting and timely.

However, I do not buy the actual setting provided in the paper (see weakness part in detail), which seems to be pretty limited and constrained. The method provided is fine, although the experiments are somehow not thorough.

Currently there are several major drawbacks and weaknesses, in terms of setting and exepriments. I view this work as a half-baked work and needs significant improvements.

In summary, in my view, the current elaboration and presentation do not meet the standards of ICLR. I am open to increase my evaluation if my principal concerns in the Weaknesses section are addressed in a convincing manner.

content.title: Domain Generalization in Regression
content.TL;DR: We propose a new domain generalization setting in regression scenario and a weighted meta-learning solution.
content.abstract: In the context of classification, \textit{domain generalization} (DG) aims to predict the labels of unseen target-domain data only using labeled source-domain data, where the source and target domains usually share \textit{the same label set}. However, in the context of regression, DG is not well studied in the literature, and the main reason is that ranges of response variable in both domains are often \textit{different}, even disjoint under some extreme conditions. In this paper, we study a new problem setting: \textit{domain generalization in regression} (DGR), and propose a weighted meta-learning strategy to get optimal meta-initialization across disjoint domains to help address the DGR problem. The motivation is that when the meta-model performs well on one domain, we hope such a model also performs well in other related domains. To measure the relatedness regarding domains in the context of regression, we use the feature discrepancy in meta-space to calculate the discrepancy between any two domains and treat the discrepancy as the weight of a meta-training task in the meta-learning framework. The extensive regression experiments on standard domain generalization benchmark demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.
